newsitem.title: USA: Coca-Cola in talks with two drink firms.
newsitem.headline: Coca-Cola in talks with two drink firms.

text.p: Coca-Cola Co. was in talks with two small private beverage firms over trademark disputes involving its new "Surge" citrus-flavored soft drink, representatives of the two companies said Thursday.
Neither company has filed trademark infringement suits against the beverage giant as yet, but both were poised to take action if no settlement was reached.
A Coca-Cola spokesman said it was going ahead with the scheduled kickoff of a $50 million advertising campaign for Surge during the Super Bowl football game on Sunday.
Surge is a high-caffeine, youth-oriented soft drink aimed at the growing market for PepsiCo Inc.'s Mountain Dew.
"We've been contacted by these parties. Beyond that we cannot comment," a spokeswoman for Atlanta-based Coca-Cola said.

One of the companies, Bio-Technology Pharmacal of Fayetteville, Ark., has held an Arkansas trademark for its "Surge" citrus-flavored health drink since 1994, and had since established its national trademark by distributing it around the country, spokesman Steve Jaffe said.
Jaffe said Coca-Cola had obtained patents on names that included the word "surge" preceded by "energy", "solar", and "power" -- but not "surge" by itself.
The other trademark case involved R.J. Corr Naturals of Posen, Ill., a Chicago suburb, which makes the ginseng-flavored drinks "Dr. Rush" and "Ginseng Rush."

The dispute focused on Coca-Cola's ad campaign created by the Leo Burnett agency featuring the slogan, "Feed the Rush", which R.J. Corr Naturals president Robert Corr said copied a consistent theme of its advertising since 1979.

Earlier Thursday, Coca-Cola settled its dispute with Babson Bros Co., a privately-held Illinois producer of milking machines and cleansers that used the "Surge" brand name on its products. Terms were not disclosed.

Babson contended that it had held a trademark on the name Surge since 1925 for its automatic milking machine and industrial cleaning products. Chairman Nick Babson had said he was concerned there might be a health risk if consumers confused its green-colored cleaning products with the new soft drink.
